lessons.title: Multicast policy NAT and VDOM loop prevention
lessons.subtitle: Separate the forwarding gate from policy matching, then prove what is translated and where the packet can exit.
lessons.summary: NAT-mode multicast forwarding is not the same thing as multicast routing. The system forwarding gate permits eligible multicast packets to be considered for forwarding; multicast-policy objects then scope the packet by ingress/egress interface, source, group, protocol and port, and can translate source or destination addresses. The most dangerous configuration is an all-to-all policy that creates a forwarding loop across NPU virtual links in a multi-VDOM design.
lessons.content_html:
Purpose and packet path

FortiGate has two distinct multicast roles. A FortiGate acting as a multicast router uses multicast-routing functions such as PIM and the routing table to build multicast distribution state. NAT-mode multicast forwarding is a different, simpler forwarding path. In that path, multicast-forward is the system-level gate. When enabled, eligible multicast packets with TTL greater than one can be forwarded out interfaces other than the ingress interface, with the TTL decremented. That behavior alone does not mean a security policy has authorized the stream. The multicast-policy table is the policy gate that scopes which stream is allowed to leave which interface.

The operational sequence is: packet arrives on an interface; the multicast-forward setting allows the NAT-mode forwarding path; FortiGate evaluates multicast-policy rules; a matching rule can apply source or destination translation; the packet exits the selected interface. A policy miss is not repaired by adding a route. Conversely, a forwarding gate that is enabled does not make every multicast group safe to flood.

Policy objects and translation

A multicast policy resembles a firewall policy but uses multicast-specific address objects and matching semantics. Its important dimensions are source interface, destination interface, source address, multicast destination group, protocol, and port range. The built-in multicast address object all represents the IPv4 multicast block 224.0.0.0/4; it is not an all-IPv4 destination object. For production, define a narrow multicast-address object for the actual group range and a host object for the sender. This avoids accidentally authorizing unrelated groups.

Source NAT is useful when receivers or an upstream network must see a stable translated source. Destination NAT changes the multicast group that receivers subscribe to or that the downstream network expects. These are separate operations: set snat enable with set snat-ip rewrites the source; set dnat rewrites the destination group. Do not use either as a substitute for choosing the correct egress interface. The translation should be driven by the receiver design, not used as a generic workaround for an incorrect multicast route.

config system settings
    set multicast-forward enable
end
config firewall multicast-policy
    edit 10
        set srcintf "encoder"
        set dstintf "receiver-net"
        set srcaddr "encoder-172.20.5.18"
        set dstaddr "239.168.4.0-255"
        set protocol 17
        set start-port 5004
        set end-port 5004
        set snat enable
        set snat-ip 192.0.2.10
        set dnat 239.168.5.10
        set logtraffic all
    next
end

The example is a policy skeleton; confirm the exact multicast address object and translation fields supported by the target FortiOS build before pasting it. Keep the interface pair explicit. A broad any destination can make troubleshooting deceptively easy while greatly widening the forwarding domain.

Why multi-VDOM designs can loop

Fortinet documents a specific hazard when multicast forwarding is enabled in multi-VDOM mode and an all-to-all multicast policy includes the NPU virtual-link interfaces in the same VDOM. A packet can be forwarded from one virtual link to the other and then back through the same policy domain. This is not a TTL problem to solve by increasing TTL. It is an interface-scope and topology problem. Use explicit source and destination interfaces and keep the NPU virtual links out of an all-to-all multicast policy. Also do not enable NAT-mode multicast forwarding when the FortiGate is operating as the multicast router; use the multicast-routing design instead.

Verification and failure isolation

Start with show system settings to prove whether multicast forwarding is enabled, then inspect show firewall multicast-policy to confirm interface, source, group, protocol, port and translation values. A matching policy entry proves that the configured rule is present; it does not prove that the stream reached the interface or that the receiver joined the group. Capture on ingress and egress and compare source and destination IPs. If the packet is present on ingress but absent on egress, check the forwarding gate, TTL, policy order and group object. If the stream exits but receivers reject it, compare the translated group/source with the receiver subscription and upstream ACLs.

For duplicate streams or a loop, capture on both NPU virtual links and inspect the policy for any interfaces. A repeated packet with the same payload and alternating virtual-link direction is stronger evidence of a loop than a rising multicast packet counter alone. In transparent mode, verify the multicast-policy behavior separately; do not assume the NAT-mode forwarding gate is the only control. The key diagnostic distinction is whether the packet was never admitted, was admitted but matched the wrong egress/translation, or was forwarded into a loop.

Dependencies and operational caveats

Multicast forwarding has platform and feature constraints, including the documented incompatibility with enhanced MAC VLAN configurations. Multicast traffic also has TTL semantics that are independent of policy NAT: a packet with TTL one cannot be forwarded by a router-like hop. Treat policy, routing, receiver membership and TTL as separate evidence layers. A successful packet capture at the FortiGate egress proves forwarding and translation; it does not prove that IGMP membership, upstream multicast routing, or the receiver application is correct.
sources: FortiOS 8.0.0 Administration Guide — Configuring multicast forwarding
FortiOS 7.6.0 Administration Guide — multicast forwarding and multi-VDOM caveat

lessons.title: FortiManager HA replication and failover boundaries
lessons.subtitle: Understand the primary/secondary state model, heartbeat timing, VRRP behavior, and settings that remain peer-local.
lessons.summary: FortiManager HA is a primary-led management database cluster, not a transparent mirror of every operating-system setting. The primary replicates module data to secondary peers over a dedicated HA path; heartbeat and data synchronization are separate operational concerns. Failover can be manual or VRRP-based, and several local settings must be maintained independently.
lessons.content_html:
Cluster roles and state replication

FortiManager HA uses one primary unit and one or more secondary units. The primary is the writable source for the managed-device database, ADOMs, policy packages, objects, scripts, and other replicated module data. A secondary is not an independent management authority that should receive routine configuration changes. When an administrator commits a change on the primary, FortiManager synchronizes the applicable module data to the peer units. Fortinet's guide describes a primary with up to four secondary peers.

Do not treat the cluster as a byte-for-byte copy of the appliance. FortiManager synchronizes database and module data, but peer-local settings remain local. The excluded or independently configured items include system hostname, time/NTP, network interfaces, backup schedules and destinations, web proxy settings, local certificates, SNMP and mail settings, syslog, SAML SSO, remote LDAP servers and remote administrator accounts, FortiCloud account details, and downloaded FortiGuard database content. Some FortiGuard deployment metadata is synchronized, but that does not mean the downloaded package database itself is copied. This is why a secondary can report synchronized module data while still lacking a usable local proxy, certificate, LDAP path, or time source.

Heartbeat versus module synchronization

FortiManager HA uses a peer connection for heartbeat and synchronization; the documented default heartbeat interval is 10 seconds and the default failover threshold is 30 missed heartbeats. That yields a nominal five-minute detection interval, not an instantaneous failover. The HA connection uses TCP port 5199 and the HA traffic is encrypted with TLS 1.3. Keep the peer path reachable and avoid sharing it with congested management traffic. A heartbeat proves that peers can exchange liveness information; it does not prove every module has completed synchronization.

The HA status view exposes module synchronization state, including Module Data Synchronized and Pending Module Data. A growing pending count means the peer has not yet caught up. A zero pending count is useful evidence for replicated module data, but it does not prove the local settings listed above are identical. Treat heartbeat status and module data status as separate health signals.

Manual and VRRP failover

In manual mode, the operator controls role promotion. A secondary does not simply take over because the primary is unreachable; the administrator must promote the peer according to the documented workflow. Manual mode is useful when the network design requires deliberate intervention, but it creates a longer recovery path and a clear human dependency. In VRRP mode, the units share a virtual IP and the secondary can become primary when the monitored interface or configured health condition fails. VRRP therefore provides automatic role movement, but it also makes interface monitoring and shared-address design critical.

Choose the mode based on the failure domain you intend to survive. If the HA heartbeat remains healthy but the primary's northbound management interface fails, VRRP monitoring can detect the service-path failure that heartbeat alone cannot see. Conversely, if the heartbeat path is lost while the primary is still serving devices, an aggressive failover threshold can create a role transition that is not aligned with actual management reachability. Tune the threshold deliberately and document which interface and IP conditions are authoritative.

Configuration and operational checks

In System Settings > HA, confirm the peer IP addresses, cluster ID, group authentication, heartbeat interface, mode, and failover settings. Keep firmware and model compatibility aligned with the supported HA design. If using VRRP, confirm the virtual IP is reachable from the managed-device network and that the monitored interface represents the service path. In manual mode, document the promotion steps and how managed FortiGates reconnect to the new primary.

For a suspected synchronization problem, compare the primary and secondary HA status, check the TCP/5199 path in both directions, and inspect module synchronization counters. Do not start by comparing every system setting in the GUI; some differences are expected because the settings are intentionally local. For FortiGuard problems, test the FDS path on both peers. The recent Community guidance on 503/504 responses and proxy tunnel mode explicitly recommends checking both HA nodes; that is an adjacent operational scenario, not the source of the HA replication feature.

Failure interpretation

If the secondary is reachable but pending module data increases, investigate synchronization and database load. If the module counters are clear but FortiGuard updates fail on the secondary, inspect its own proxy, egress and contract path. If a promoted peer cannot manage devices, verify the FGFM address, routing, certificates and management-plane reachability rather than assuming the database is corrupt. HA continuity depends on replicated management state plus peer-local service readiness.
sources: FortiManager 8.0.0 Administration Guide — Synchronizing configuration and HA heartbeat
FortiManager 8.0.0 Administration Guide — Configuring HA options
Community scenario — FDS 503/504 and proxy mode; scenario only

lessons.title: Privacy masking and time-bounded unmasking
lessons.subtitle: Mask fields per administrator profile without confusing UI visibility, historical time windows, and exported log content.
lessons.summary: FortiAnalyzer privacy masking is an administrator-profile control that anonymizes selected user and host fields across modules and reports. A Data Mask Key enables selective unmasking, while a 0–365 day window determines how historical data is presented. Real-time logs and downloaded output have different boundaries that matter during investigations.
lessons.content_html:
What the control protects

Privacy masking lets an administrator work with logs while hiding selected identity-bearing fields. It is configured in an administrator profile, not as a global log-ingestion transformation. Typical selectable fields include destination name, source IP, destination IP, user, source name, email, message, and source MAC. When the profile is assigned to an administrator, those fields are anonymized wherever the selected fields are displayed, including reports generated by that administrator. The anonymized value is different for each administrator and changes at each login, reducing the chance that a stable token can be used to identify the original user across sessions.

This is a presentation and access-control boundary, not a replacement for source-data retention controls. The underlying logs still exist for authorized processing. The profile determines what the operator can see by default and whether the operator can reveal a selected value with the configured Data Mask Key. Because the mask is profile-scoped, two administrators looking at the same event can see different representations depending on their assigned profiles.

Configuration sequence

Go to System Settings > Admin Profiles and create or edit a profile. Enable Privacy Masking, select the fields to mask, set the Data Mask Key, and choose Data Unmasked Time from 0 to 365 days. Then go to System Settings > Administrators and assign that profile to the intended administrator. If a required field is not available in the GUI list, Fortinet documents adding fields through the CLI. Treat the key as a privileged secret: the administrator needs it to reveal original values, so it should not be distributed to every user who can view masked logs.

The time setting is easy to misread. If the Log View time range extends beyond the configured unmasked period, historical data is masked. For example, with a seven-day window, a query covering the last 30 days masks values outside the permitted window. This is a time-range rule, not a row limit. The profile can therefore show the same event differently depending on the selected time range.

Unmasking and export behavior

In a list that contains masked data, the administrator can select See Original Data and choose Screen Picker or Manual Input. Screen Picker copies the selected masked field into the unmask dialog; Manual Input allows the operator to enter the masked text. The Data Mask Key from the profile is then required. Only the selected field is revealed; other masked fields remain anonymized. This is a deliberate, field-level reveal rather than a blanket switch that turns privacy masking off for the entire administrator.

A critical operational trap is the download path. FortiAnalyzer allows a privacy-masked administrator to download logs from Log View, but masked data is excluded from the downloaded output. Seeing an original value in the GUI after using See Original Data does not prove the exported file contains that value. If an investigation requires a raw export, use an explicitly authorized process and validate the output rather than assuming the GUI reveal changed the export behavior.

Time-frame boundaries and verification

The Data Unmasked Time setting accepts whole numbers from 0 to 365. The time-frame masking rule does not apply to real-time logs; it applies to custom-view and drill-down data. That distinction matters when an operator compares a real-time pane with a historical custom view and sees different masking behavior. Do not interpret the difference as a logging or database corruption issue before checking the view type and query time range.

Validate with two test administrators assigned different profiles. Use the same event and compare the selected fields. Confirm that the masked profile sees anonymous values, that a fresh login changes the anonymized representation, and that the Data Mask Key reveals only the selected value. Then test a time range inside and outside the configured window, compare real-time and custom-view results, and download a log to confirm masked fields are omitted. The evidence should demonstrate each boundary separately.

Operational safeguards

Keep the Data Mask Key out of shared notes and general administrator profiles. Assign the least-privilege profile to analysts who need trends and event context but do not need personal identifiers. Use a separate controlled process for authorized unmasking and raw evidence export. Privacy masking supports privacy requirements, but it does not remove the need to control administrator permissions, report distribution, retention, and the handling of unmasked values.
sources: FortiAnalyzer 8.0.0 Administration Guide — Creating administrator profiles
FortiAnalyzer 7.6.6 Administration Guide — Administrator profile field list

lessons.title: IP conflict detection with passive ARP and active GARP
lessons.subtitle: Understand the two detection triggers and the difference between a passive trap and an active probe log.
lessons.summary: FortiSwitch IP conflict detection protects system-interface addresses, not every endpoint address in every VLAN. It combines passive observation of remote ARP claims with active gratuitous-ARP probes after local interface events. The evidence and notification behavior differ between the two methods.
lessons.content_html:
Purpose and scope

FortiSwitch IP conflict detection identifies another device claiming an IP address already assigned to a FortiSwitch system interface. It is useful for management-interface conflicts that can make the switch unreachable or cause management traffic to reach the wrong MAC address. It is not a general IP address management scanner and should not be described as continuous detection of every host-to-host duplicate address in the access VLANs.

The global detect-ip-conflict setting is enabled by default in the documented FortiSwitchOS behavior. The feature has two distinct detection paths: passive detection observes ARP traffic that is already present on the network; active detection generates a gratuitous ARP (GARP) probe when a relevant local interface event occurs. Because the triggers differ, the expected logs and traps are not identical.

Passive detection: observe a remote claim

In the passive path, the switch listens for broadcast ARP packets. It compares the sender IP address in the ARP packet with the IP addresses configured on its system interfaces. If a remote device claims one of those addresses, FortiSwitch records a conflict. The documentation describes a system log and an SNMP trap for this passive detection path. This is useful because the switch does not need to initiate a probe; it can detect a conflict when the duplicate device announces itself.

Passive detection depends on the ARP claim being visible to the switch. A quiet duplicate device that never sends an observable ARP announcement may not be detected immediately. The feature is therefore not a substitute for DHCP reservation management or a full duplicate-address detection system across all endpoints.

Active detection: probe after local events

The active path is triggered when the system boots, when a system interface transitions from down to up, or when a local system-interface IP address changes. FortiSwitch sends a GARP probe to announce the local address. If another device responds as the owner of the same IP, the switch records a conflict in the system log. The documented active response is a log message; do not assume that every active probe response produces the same SNMP trap described for passive ARP detection.

This distinction is important during a maintenance window. If an engineer changes the management IP and sees a conflict log immediately after the interface comes up, the event may have been generated by the active GARP path. If a trap arrives while the switch is otherwise idle, inspect the passive ARP path and the packet that claimed the address.

Configuration and evidence

Check the global setting with the FortiSwitchOS system configuration and keep detection enabled unless there is a documented reason to change it. The relevant setting is detect-ip-conflict. Configure the SNMP trap receiver and confirm that the FortiSwitch is allowed to send notifications to it. For passive detection, correlate the system log and trap timestamp with an ARP capture showing the sender IP and MAC. For active detection, correlate the log with boot, interface-up, or IP-change events and capture the GARP probe/reply exchange.

A useful evidence chain is: local interface configuration, conflict log text, ARP/GARP packet, and switch forwarding-table entry for the responding MAC. The log proves FortiSwitch detected a duplicate claim; it does not by itself identify the physical location of the other device. Use the MAC address in the ARP reply and the CAM table to trace the port. If the duplicate is a DHCP client, inspect the DHCP lease and reservation; if it is a static device, correct the static address or the FortiSwitch management address.

Operational troubleshooting

If the switch management address is duplicated, do not immediately change the switch IP and assume the problem is solved. First determine which device owns the duplicate address and whether the conflicting device is using a stale static configuration, a reused DHCP reservation, or a cloned management configuration. Check whether the conflict is on the management interface, a VLAN interface, or another system interface. After correction, clear any stale ARP state on the relevant upstream devices and verify that the FortiSwitch management MAC is again the only owner.

For monitoring, alert on the specific IP-conflict log and SNMP trap rather than on all ARP activity. A lack of trap does not prove that active GARP detection did not run; check the system log for that path. Conversely, a trap proves passive detection fired, not that the switch has scanned every host in the subnet.
sources: FortiSwitchOS 8.0.0 Administration Guide — IP conflict detection
FortiSwitchOS 8.0.0 CLI Reference — system global setting

lessons.title: WPA3 Beacon Protection and over-the-air verification
lessons.subtitle: A VAP setting is not enough: the VAP must reach the active radio profile and the beacon must carry its MIC.
lessons.summary: Beacon Protection protects the integrity of WPA3 beacon frames. FortiAP adds a Management MIC element and advertises the capability in Extended Capabilities. The feature is disabled by default, limited to supported Wi-Fi 6E/Wi-Fi 7 hardware and firmware, and requires both VAP configuration and WTP-profile assignment.
lessons.content_html:
Why beacon integrity matters

Beacon frames are management frames that advertise an SSID and provide information clients use during network discovery and connection establishment. If a client accepts a forged beacon, it can be misled about the network it is discovering. Beacon Protection adds integrity protection to the beacon frame so a client can validate that the beacon came from an entity possessing the appropriate keying material. This is not the same thing as protecting every management frame or encrypting user data; it is a specific integrity enhancement for beacon frames.

Fortinet documents Beacon Protection for WPA3 SSIDs and supports it on FortiAP Wi-Fi 6E and Wi-Fi 7 models running FAP 7.6.1 or later. It is disabled by default. A WPA3 SSID or PMF setting alone does not prove Beacon Protection is active. The VAP setting must be enabled and the VAP must be assigned to the WTP profile radio that is actually serving the SSID.

Configuration path

On the FortiGate wireless controller, edit the WPA3 VAP under config wireless-controller vap. The documented example enables PMF and Beacon Protection:

config wireless-controller vap
    edit "wpa3-sae-beacon"
        set security wpa3-only-enterprise
        set pmf enable
        set beacon-protection enable
        set auth radius
        set radius-server "peap"
    next
end

Next, assign the VAP to the intended radio in the WTP profile. The Fortinet example assigns the VAP under config radio-2 and set vaps. That second step matters. A VAP can be correctly configured in the controller database but absent from the radio profile used by a particular AP. The AP will then not transmit the protected SSID on that radio.

Runtime verification

Use vcfg on the FortiAP to inspect the VAP runtime configuration. The example output includes pmf=required and beacon_prot=enabled. This proves the AP instantiated the configured VAP with Beacon Protection enabled. It does not prove a client associated successfully or that the client validates the MIC.

For packet-level verification, capture beacon frames over the air for the target BSSID. Fortinet's example shows a Management MIC element (tag number 76) with a 16-byte length, KeyID, IPN and MIC fields. The 11th octet of the Extended Capabilities element carries the Beacon Protection flag. Seeing both the Management MIC and the capability flag is stronger evidence than a GUI checkbox because it proves the AP is transmitting the protected beacon format.

Failure isolation

If vcfg shows beacon_prot=disabled or no VAP entry, verify the AP model, FAP version, VAP configuration, and WTP profile assignment. Confirm the SSID is WPA3 and PMF is enabled. Check that the profile is assigned to the AP and the correct radio is active. If runtime output says enabled but the capture lacks the MIC, capture the correct BSSID and verify that the capture is not showing a neighboring AP or an old beacon. A packet capture from the wrong radio can make a correct configuration appear broken.

If the feature is unavailable in the GUI or CLI, verify hardware and firmware support before changing unrelated wireless settings. The documented model/firmware boundary is not bypassed by a FortiGuard subscription or a client driver update. Also remember that Beacon Protection is not a replacement for PMF, WPA3 authentication, client security, or RF planning. It strengthens beacon integrity; it does not fix weak passwords, rogue AP placement, or poor channel design.

Operational interpretation

Use three separate checks: controller configuration, AP runtime configuration, and over-the-air beacon content. A successful first check proves intent; the second proves the AP accepted and instantiated the configuration; the third proves the expected beacon fields are actually on the air. If a client still fails to connect, move to WPA3 authentication, RADIUS, PMF negotiation and client capability rather than assuming the beacon MIC itself is the cause.
sources: FortiAP 7.6.5 Configuration Guide — Enabling Beacon Protection
FortiGate 7.4.0 New Features — Wi-Fi 7 profile support

lessons.title: Access Point Management using DHCP and DNS state enforcement
lessons.subtitle: Control hosts behind bridging APs and hubs when per-client VLAN switching is unavailable.
lessons.summary: FortiNAC Access Point Management uses DHCP address pools and DNS behavior to distinguish authorized and unauthorized hosts behind non-VLAN-aware APs or hubs. The AP uplink is treated as an access point management port; DHCP lease state drives the host path, while DNS directs unauthorized hosts to a state-specific portal.
lessons.content_html:
When this feature is useful

Some wireless access points and small hubs bridge multiple endpoints into one upstream VLAN but cannot place each client into a different VLAN. In that topology, a NAC design that depends on dynamic VLAN assignment per endpoint cannot enforce host state at the edge. FortiNAC Access Point Management provides an alternate control path: it uses DHCP pools and DNS responses to steer hosts into an authorized or restricted experience while they remain behind the same bridging AP or hub.

The feature is a FortiNAC 9.4 procedure. Do not copy the exact workflow into FortiNAC-F without checking that product's own guide and release support. The control plane and UI differ between the product families.

Network and port prerequisites

The AP uplink must be visible to FortiNAC through the upstream switch. The port is placed in the Access Point Management group, and the AP must not remain classified as a generic Bridging Device. The documented workflow removes the AP from the Bridging Devices group and removes any user-defined uplink classification that would cause FortiNAC to treat the AP as a different infrastructure object. After changing the group, synchronize the switch configuration so the port role is current.

In the FortiNAC Configuration Wizard, define the Access Point Management VLAN and the address ranges for the authorized and unauthorized pools. The upstream DHCP relay must forward requests to FortiNAC. The AP management view also needs DNS settings: authorized hosts receive production DNS, while unauthorized hosts receive the FortiNAC AP-management DNS path. That DNS path resolves the portal/redirection destination to the FortiNAC Application Server, which can present the appropriate portal based on the host's state.

DHCP and DNS transaction

When a host behind the AP requests an address, FortiNAC uses the host's known state and DHCP lease information to determine which pool should answer. An authorized host receives an address from the authorized range and a DNS configuration that resolves normal production names. An unauthorized or unregistered host receives an address from the restricted range and the AP-management DNS server. DNS queries are then redirected to the FortiNAC Application Server, which can send the user to registration, remediation, quarantine, or another state-specific portal.

This is not a per-host VLAN change. The same AP uplink and shared VLAN carry multiple clients; the separation is achieved through DHCP and DNS behavior. The feature is therefore sensitive to whether the endpoint actually uses DHCP and whether the relay path is correct. A static-IP host may not appear in the expected DHCP lease file.

Static addressing and event handling

FortiNAC documents a StaticIPAddress event for hosts that are not represented in the DHCP lease file but appear to be using a static address. Map that event to an alarm and action if the operational policy requires investigation or remediation. Do not assume that the feature automatically disables a static-IP host; event generation and the configured alarm/action determine the response. The lease file, DHCP relay, and event mapping are therefore important evidence sources.

Verification and troubleshooting

Verify the AP is connected to the intended upstream switch port, the port is in the Access Point Management group, and the AP is not still in Bridging Devices. Confirm the DHCP relay points to FortiNAC and that both address pools are configured. Test with one known authorized host and one unregistered host. Compare the offered address, gateway and DNS server. Resolve a normal internal name from the authorized host; from the unauthorized host, verify the AP-management DNS path resolves to the Application Server and that the correct portal appears.

A documented limitation is important during rescans: if a host fails a rescan while it is still on the production network, FortiNAC may not move it to the isolated path until the existing lease expires or the host disconnects and renews. A successful alarm alone does not prove the endpoint has changed DNS or address pools. Check the current lease and force a clean DHCP renewal when safe. If the host uses a static IP, verify that the StaticIPAddress event is mapped to an action rather than expecting a DHCP transition.

Operational caveats

Access Point Management is best viewed as a DHCP/DNS-based fallback for infrastructure that cannot perform per-client VLAN assignment. It is not a substitute for 802.1X where the AP and switching fabric support it. It also does not guarantee that an endpoint cannot manually configure a static address; that condition must be detected and handled through event policy and upstream controls. Document the DHCP lease duration because it affects how quickly a failed rescan changes the endpoint's actual network path.
sources: FortiNAC 9.4.0 Administration Guide — Access Point Management
FortiNAC Community — Configuring Access Point Management (historical scenario, 2023-04-25)

lessons.title: Machine authentication with Active Directory compute-group RBAC
lessons.subtitle: Separate the computer identity from the interactive user and map the host into an ordinary LDAP group.
lessons.summary: FortiNAC-F machine authentication uses the endpoint's computer identity or EAP-TLS certificate during 802.1X. Directory synchronization can create a host-group mapping with a `_host` suffix so a machine is assigned to a compute group independently of a user's interactive login. Primary AD groups are not supported for this mapping.
lessons.content_html:
Why machine authentication is a separate decision

In 802.1X deployments, the network may need to authorize a domain-joined workstation before any user signs in. That is different from authenticating the person who later logs on. Machine authentication proves that the endpoint has a valid computer identity or certificate and can therefore receive the network access policy intended for managed corporate devices. If the design only evaluates the interactive user, a workstation may have no usable network path during boot, domain logon, software deployment, or policy refresh.

FortiNAC-F 7.6 provides a machine-authentication workflow that can use Active Directory compute groups for RBAC. The directory synchronization behavior creates a host-group mapping with a _host suffix. For example, an LDAP group named Engineering can be represented as Engineering_host for host identity assignment. The group attribute must be configured to use the host-group mapping so that the computer record, rather than an interactive user record, receives the membership.

Authentication methods and RADIUS path

The endpoint initiates 802.1X and the switch or AP forwards the exchange to FortiNAC-F's local RADIUS server. The machine identity can be validated using the computer account credentials with MSCHAPv2 or by presenting a client certificate with EAP-TLS. These paths have different dependencies. MSCHAPv2 relies on the computer account and the configured domain integration; EAP-TLS relies on the client certificate, the issuing CA chain, and the RADIUS server's TLS certificate configuration.

For EAP-TLS, create the certificate request through FortiNAC-F certificate management, have the enterprise CA sign it, and upload the signed certificate. Add the AD root CA to the trusted certificates and select the appropriate certificate on the local RADIUS server. The Windows client must be configured to use the intended EAP method and trust the issuing CA. For MSCHAPv2, confirm that the endpoint is domain joined and that the Winbind/domain integration is healthy. A valid user login does not prove that the computer account path is working.

Directory-group mapping and a common trap

Synchronize the LDAP directory and inspect the Groups view. The host group is represented with the _host suffix. Fortinet documents a limitation with primary Active Directory groups such as Domain Computers: primary groups are not supported for this mapping. A common failed design is to select Domain Computers, see no expected host-group membership, and then change the EAP method. The actual issue is the directory group type. Create an ordinary LDAP security group, add the computer accounts to it, synchronize again, and use the resulting host-group mapping.

Keep the group attribute and host record relationship explicit. The group mapping is not a switch-port identity, a RADIUS client name, or a FortiGate configuration template. It is a directory-backed RBAC membership applied to the host identity after machine authentication and directory synchronization.

Certificate identity and version boundaries

When EAP-TLS is used, inspect the certificate subject and SAN values that FortiNAC-F uses to associate the certificate with the endpoint. The Client Certificate Attribute enhancement is available starting in FortiNAC-F 7.6.3. It allows the administrator to select an attribute such as CN, DNS, or UPN when extracting the hostname. If the setting is not available on an earlier release, do not assume it is hidden by an RBAC permission; verify the deployed version. Without the enhancement, the certificate subject and hostname conventions must already align with the documented machine-authentication workflow.

Verification and troubleshooting

Use a known domain-joined test workstation. Confirm the machine authentication exchange in the RADIUS log, check the certificate chain if EAP-TLS is used, and inspect the FortiNAC-F host record. Verify the expected _host group appears after directory synchronization. If the RADIUS authentication succeeds but the host is assigned to the wrong group, inspect the group attribute and LDAP membership rather than the switch VLAN. If no host record is created, check the machine identity presented by the endpoint, domain join status, Winbind state, and certificate hostname mapping.

For a certificate failure, separate three questions: did the client present a certificate, did FortiNAC-F trust the issuing chain, and did the certificate identity map to the expected host? A certificate can be valid in a browser and still fail EAP-TLS if the RADIUS service is configured with a different server certificate or the client does not trust the issuing CA. The operational goal is a reproducible machine identity, a correct host-group membership, and an access decision that does not depend on a human user being logged in.

lessons.title: FIDO authentication for IdP-initiated SAML
lessons.subtitle: The FIDO challenge authenticates at the IdP; service-provider visibility and assertion acceptance remain separate controls.
lessons.summary: FortiAuthenticator 8.0.2 adds FIDO authentication for IdP-initiated SAML login. The user starts at the FortiAuthenticator IdP portal, completes the configured FIDO/password method, selects an authorized service provider, and receives a SAML assertion response. FIDO success is not proof that the SP has authorized the user or accepted the assertion.
lessons.content_html:
Where FIDO fits in the SAML transaction

In an IdP-initiated SAML flow, the user starts at the identity provider rather than at the service provider. FortiAuthenticator presents its IdP portal, authenticates the user, displays the service providers available to that user, and sends an assertion response to the selected SP. FortiAuthenticator 8.0.2 adds an IdP Initiated Login configuration pane that can require FIDO authentication. The 8.0.3 SAML IdP guide describes the current portal behavior and service-provider configuration.

When FIDO is required, the user can begin with a username-only Login Fido Page. That page identifies the account so FortiAuthenticator can apply the configured authentication method. Depending on the configuration, the user completes FIDO alone or a password-plus-FIDO sequence. A fallback option can be used when the user's FIDO keys have all been revoked, but fallback must be an intentional policy decision rather than an assumed bypass.

Service-provider configuration is a separate gate

After successful IdP authentication, the user sees the list of service providers they are allowed to launch. Each SP must be configured to support IdP-initiated assertion responses. If that setting is disabled, the SP may not appear in the portal even though the user has a valid FIDO credential. User-source and group filters can also restrict which users see a particular SP. This is an authorization and portal-visibility decision, not a FIDO failure.

The complete flow is: browser reaches the FortiAuthenticator IdP portal; username identifies the user; FIDO/password factors are evaluated; the SP list is filtered by authorization; the user selects an SP; FortiAuthenticator creates and signs the SAML assertion; the browser posts it to the SP's assertion consumer service; the SP validates the issuer, signature, audience, recipient, time conditions and user attributes before creating its own session.

Configuration and evidence

In Authentication > SAML IdP > General, configure the IdP-initiated login method and select the FIDO behavior appropriate to the user population. Ensure users have enrolled a FIDO credential and that the required login page/message is configured. In the Service Providers section, confirm IdP-initiated assertion response support is enabled for the target SP. Review the user source and group filters that determine whether the SP is displayed. A successful FIDO event proves the user passed the IdP factor; it does not prove the SP's ACS URL, signing certificate, audience, or NameID mapping is correct.

For troubleshooting, test the flow in stages. If the username-only page appears but FIDO fails, check enrollment, authenticator registration, browser support, and whether the account is configured for FIDO-only or password-plus-FIDO. If FIDO succeeds but the SP is absent, check SP enablement and user authorization filters. If the SP appears and the browser posts an assertion but the SP rejects it, inspect the SAML response at the SP: issuer, signature certificate, audience, recipient, destination, validity window, NameID and attribute mapping.

Common diagnostic mistakes

Do not treat a missing SP as a failed FIDO challenge. Do not assume a successful FIDO prompt means the user has access to every SP. Do not change the SP's ACS URL to fix a credential-enrollment problem. These are separate layers in the transaction. Also distinguish IdP-initiated from SP-initiated login: the browser entry point and the SP request context differ, so an SP-initiated troubleshooting procedure may not explain an IdP portal failure.

Operational safeguards

Keep FIDO enrollment and revocation processes current. If fallback to password and OTP is permitted when keys are revoked, document how that fallback is audited and who can invoke it. Test both the normal FIDO path and the recovery path. Use a test SP with a known signing certificate and predictable user mapping before rolling the setting to production applications. This isolates the IdP factor from the SP assertion-processing layer.

lessons.title: Kerberos authentication for native RDP Network Level Authentication
lessons.subtitle: Use the secret's domain to derive the Kerberos realm, then verify KDC discovery and the native-launcher boundary.
lessons.summary: FortiPAM 1.9.0 supports Kerberos for native RDP sessions that use NLA/CredSSP. The secret or target domain supplies the Kerberos realm; FortiPAM discovers the KDC through DNS SRV unless an administrator configures an explicit KDC address. The feature does not apply to Web RDP.
lessons.content_html:
Why use Kerberos for RDP NLA

Network Level Authentication requires authentication before the full RDP session is established. FortiPAM's native RDP launcher can use Kerberos rather than the default NTLM behavior when the secret is configured for NLA and Use Kerberos for NLA is enabled. This is useful in modern Active Directory environments where Kerberos is the preferred authentication method and where reducing NTLM use is part of the security design.

FortiPAM derives the Kerberos realm from the domain associated with the secret or its target. In a typical AD environment, the Kerberos realm follows the DNS name of the Windows domain. When the native launcher starts, FortiPAM uses the domain and credential information to request a Kerberos ticket from the appropriate Key Distribution Center (KDC). This means that target naming and domain configuration are part of the authentication transaction, not just metadata for the secret vault.

Configuration sequence

In Secrets > Secrets, edit the secret and open the RDP Service pane. Enable the RDP service, set RDP Security Level to NLA, and enable Use Kerberos for NLA. If NLA is not selected, the Kerberos option does not apply. When the option is disabled, FortiPAM uses the default NLA authentication behavior, which is NTLM in the documented configuration.

For KDC discovery, FortiPAM uses DNS SRV records for the Kerberos realm when no explicit KDC Address is configured. In Secrets > Targets, Advanced Domain Settings includes KDC Address. An administrator can specify an FQDN or IP address and an optional port; the default is 88. Use an explicit KDC only when DNS SRV discovery is unsuitable or the deployment requires a specific KDC. A manually entered KDC address does not correct an incorrect realm or target domain.

Fortinet recommends using a Target Only secret with the target computer FQDN as host information, associated with the corresponding Windows Domain Account secret. Another documented pattern is a Windows Domain Account secret template with the target FQDN entered when the RDP session is launched. Both patterns make the domain and target identity explicit.

Transaction and dependencies

The native RDP launcher begins the NLA/CredSSP exchange. FortiPAM uses the secret's domain to construct the Kerberos realm, locates the KDC through DNS SRV or the explicit KDC Address, and requests the ticket with the associated credentials. The target then participates in the NLA exchange. The target FQDN matters because Kerberos service identity is tied to the domain and service principal, while an IP-only target can obscure the intended host identity.

Check DNS SRV resolution for the realm, KDC reachability on the configured port (normally 88), domain correctness, credential validity, and time synchronization between the FortiPAM environment, KDC and target. If DNS SRV returns the wrong domain controller or no record, test an explicit KDC Address as a diagnostic step. Do not leave a hard-coded KDC in place without documenting the dependency and failover behavior.

Launcher limitations and TCP forwarding

Kerberos authentication is supported only for the native RDP launcher. It is not a Web RDP feature. FortiPAM 1.9.0 also introduced TCP Forwarding for native RDP launch. That option routes the traffic through the generic TCP-forwarding path and removes support for RDP Security Level, Restricted Admin Mode, Auto TOTP and Block Clipboard. Do not enable TCP Forwarding as a generic workaround while expecting the NLA/Kerberos controls to remain available.

Evidence-driven troubleshooting

Confirm the secret shows RDP enabled, Security Level NLA, and Use Kerberos for NLA enabled. Confirm the target has the expected domain and KDC Address (or that DNS SRV records resolve). Check network reachability to the KDC and target. Then test with the native launcher and a known Windows Domain Account secret. If the option is unavailable or has no effect, verify that the session is using the native RDP launcher and that TCP Forwarding is not changing the path.

A successful TCP connection to the target proves only that the RDP service is reachable. It does not prove that the KDC can issue a ticket or that the realm and target identity align. A successful Kerberos ticket request proves the KDC path; the final NLA result proves the target accepted the credential exchange. Keep these stages separate when diagnosing failures.

FortiPAM 1.9.0 Administration Guide — Creating a secret

lessons.title: Federated Search across external data stores
lessons.subtitle: Provider credentials, dataset definitions and observable-to-column mappings determine whether an external hunt returns meaningful results.
lessons.summary: FortiSIEM 7.5 Federated Search lets a ClickHouse deployment query supported external data stores such as AWS Security Lake, S3, FortiEDR, PostgreSQL, MySQL and Snowflake. Providers, datasets/tables and observable mappings are separate configuration objects; successful connectivity alone does not prove the search maps the correct columns.
lessons.content_html:
Purpose and deployment boundary

Federated Search lets an analyst pivot from a FortiSIEM incident or analytics result into external telemetry without first normalizing every external record into the ordinary event-ingestion pipeline. It is a 7.5 feature for ClickHouse deployments. If the deployment is not using ClickHouse, the feature is not available; do not troubleshoot a missing menu as a role-permission issue until the deployment type is confirmed.

Supported external sources documented for the feature include AWS Security Lake, AWS S3, FortiEDR, PostgreSQL, MySQL and Snowflake. Each source has its own provider configuration and credential requirements. For example, AWS Security Lake access depends on the configured AWS account and the permissions required to read the relevant S3/SQS-backed data. A successful credential test is only the first step; FortiSIEM still needs to know which datastore/table to query and which external columns correspond to its normalized observables.

Three configuration layers

The first layer is the provider. It contains the connection method and credentials for the external service. The second layer is the dataset or table definition. It identifies the external data collection that can be queried. The third layer is the observable mapping. FortiSIEM uses normalized observable types such as Source IP Address, Destination IP Address, host name, user, or process information. The mapping tells Federated Search which external column contains each observable. A provider can be reachable while the dataset is wrong; a dataset can be correct while the observable mapping points to the wrong column or data type.

Build the configuration in that order: configure the provider; define the datastore/table; map FortiSIEM observables to the external columns; save and deploy the configuration; then execute a search. When a provider or dataset definition changes, verify that the configuration is applied to the ClickHouse data nodes. A partially deployed provider can produce different behavior depending on which node handles the query.

How an analyst runs a federated query

An analyst can start from an incident or analytics result. Select a relevant field such as Source IP, create the filter, and invoke Federated Search. FortiSIEM carries the observable value into the external query. Alternatively, the analyst can open Analytics > Federated Search, select the configured datasets, choose observables and operators, specify values and a time range, and run the query. Multiple conditions can be combined with AND/OR logic. Dataset-specific result limits and time-range constraints matter; FortiEDR datasets, for example, can have a configured absolute time range that limits what can be queried.

The external query returns data into FortiSIEM. The result is stored in ClickHouse and can then be used in Advanced Search, exported to PDF or email, or attached to a case. This is the reason a federated result can be queried after the external search completes: FortiSIEM has persisted the result set rather than relying on the browser's temporary response.

Observable mapping example

Suppose an incident contains Source IP 203.0.113.44. In the external security lake, the column may be named src_ip_addr rather than Source IP Address. The mapping connects the FortiSIEM Source IP observable to src_ip_addr. If the mapping points to a destination column or a string field with a different representation, the provider can connect successfully and the search can still return no rows. Test with a known indicator and compare the raw external record with the observable mapping before changing the incident filter.

Verification and failure isolation

When Federated Search is unavailable, confirm the deployment uses ClickHouse. When the provider cannot connect, check credentials, endpoint reachability, account permissions and provider-specific configuration. When the provider connects but the dataset is empty, check the selected datastore/table and time range. When the dataset returns records but the observable filter returns none, inspect the observable-to-column mapping, data type and value normalization. When one node fails but another works, verify that the latest provider/dataset configuration has been deployed to all ClickHouse data nodes.

Do not treat a successful provider test as proof that the query semantics are correct. Do not assume a field name in an external table automatically maps to the FortiSIEM observable of the same apparent meaning. The feature's value depends on the normalized observable layer: the analyst should be able to pivot on Source IP or Destination IP consistently even when external sources use different column names and schemas.

Operational design

Use least-privilege credentials for each provider, keep external schemas stable, and version-control the observable mappings. Record the source table, time range and result limit in the case so another analyst can reproduce the hunt. Federated Search is an enrichment and investigation path; it does not replace ordinary FortiSIEM event ingestion, retention, parser development, or normalization where persistent correlation is required.

FortiSIEM 7.5.1 User Guide — Creating Federated Search from Incidents or Analytics

lessons.title: HTTP/3 QUIC inspection and traffic-scope boundaries
lessons.subtitle: Choose Inspect, Bypass, or Block deliberately, and distinguish agent/edge traffic from proxy-policy traffic.
lessons.summary: FortiSASE exposes an HTTP/3 QUIC action in the security profile group. Inspect permits HTTP/3 traffic to be inspected, Bypass permits it without inspection, and Block rejects QUIC so most clients fall back to HTTP/2. The setting applies to agent and authorized Edge-device traffic, not proxy-policy traffic.
lessons.content_html:
Why HTTP/3 changes the inspection path

HTTP/3 uses QUIC over UDP, commonly UDP/443, rather than the TCP-based transport used by HTTP/2. A security policy that assumes every browser session uses TCP/443 can therefore miss the protocol negotiation path. FortiSASE adds a specific action for HTTP/3 QUIC traffic within the security profile group's SSL-inspection settings. This allows the administrator to decide whether QUIC should be inspected, bypassed, or blocked so that the client uses a different HTTP version.

The scope is important. The documented action applies to FortiClient agent traffic and traffic from authorized Edge devices. It does not apply to proxy-policy traffic. A proxy user can therefore behave differently from an agent-based user even when both reach the same website. Do not infer that the FortiSASE HTTP/3 action is applied to every remote-user mode simply because the traffic passes through the same security PoP.

Inspect, Bypass, and Block

Inspect allows HTTP/3 and subjects it to the applicable inspection path. Use it when the organization wants HTTP/3 performance while retaining the security controls supported by the selected inspection profile. Bypass allows QUIC without inspection. This preserves the protocol but gives up the inspection path for that traffic. Block blocks HTTP/3 QUIC; most browsers then fall back to HTTP/2 over TLS/TCP, allowing the administrator to use the HTTP/2 inspection path. The fallback is client behavior, not a FortiSASE guarantee for every application.

Configure the action in Security > Traffic > Security Profile Groups, then edit the SSL inspection settings for the profile group. Confirm the profile group is actually assigned to the policy handling the agent or Edge-device traffic. A correct setting in an unused profile group has no effect on the production path.

Inspection prerequisites and client behavior

HTTP/3 inspection is tied to the SSL-inspection feature and the selected inspection mode. Verify that the profile group has the appropriate certificate or deep-inspection configuration and that endpoint trust is in place when certificate inspection is required. If the traffic is blocked, observe the browser's negotiated protocol. A browser may retry using HTTP/2, but the timing and fallback behavior can vary by application and browser version.

Proxy-policy traffic is a separate path. If a proxy user must be inspected using HTTP/2, the browser may need QUIC disabled so it does not continue attempting HTTP/3 outside the agent/edge action scope. Do not assume a FortiSASE agent profile setting controls a proxy user's browser transport. The endpoint's browser policy and the FortiSASE proxy path must be considered together.

Verification and troubleshooting

Start by classifying the endpoint: FortiClient agent, authorized Edge device, or proxy user. Then inspect the security profile group attached to the policy and confirm the HTTP/3 action. On the client, use browser developer tools and inspect the Protocol column; h3 indicates HTTP/3, while h2 indicates HTTP/2. A UDP/443 session is suggestive but not definitive proof of HTTP/3 inspection. Correlate the session with FortiSASE logs and a packet capture when the negotiated protocol is unclear.

If the administrator selected Block and the browser still appears to use QUIC, verify that the traffic is in the agent/edge scope and that the expected profile group is applied. If the browser changes to HTTP/2, that proves fallback occurred; it does not prove the HTTP/2 session is being deep-inspected. Check the SSL-inspection mode, certificate trust, security profile group and policy assignment. If the user is in proxy mode, configure browser QUIC behavior separately.

Operational design

Choose the action based on the security requirement rather than a blanket assumption that QUIC is always bad. Inspect retains the HTTP/3 path where supported; Bypass is a performance/compatibility choice with an inspection trade-off; Block is a controlled fallback strategy. Pilot the setting with agent and Edge-device users, then test proxy users separately. Record the expected browser protocol and the security controls that should see the traffic so that a protocol fallback is not mistaken for a security inspection success.
sources: FortiSASE Feature Administration Guide — Configuring an action for HTTP/3 (QUIC) traffic
FortiSASE 26.1.107 Feature Administration Guide — SSL inspection

lessons.title: Dual-server Performance SLA target fallback
lessons.subtitle: A second probe target protects against false link-down when one remote server fails independently of the path.
lessons.summary: A FortiOS Performance SLA can use up to two probe servers. FortiGate uses the first target, switches to the second when the first is unavailable, and returns to the first after the second becomes unavailable. The health check fails only when both targets are unavailable; this is distinct from SLA quality thresholds and multiple independent health checks.
lessons.content_html:
Health check, target, and SLA are different objects

A Performance SLA has three parts: health checks, SLA targets, and link status. The health check defines the probe mode, protocol and server. Participants are SD-WAN member interfaces that are expected to carry the service traffic. The SLA target defines acceptable latency, jitter and packet loss for the application. Link status defines how frequently the member is evaluated and how many failed or successful checks are required before the member becomes inactive or active again.

The server is not simply a generic internet ping destination. Fortinet recommends choosing an IP address or FQDN that reflects the resource whose path is being measured. A health check for voice should use a resource representative of voice service; a database replication check should use a resource representative of that path. The server can be an IP address or FQDN, and up to two servers can be configured in one health check.

How the two-server behavior works

When two servers are configured, FortiGate uses the first server as the probe target. If that server becomes unavailable, FortiGate switches to the second server. It remains on the second server until that server becomes unavailable, then returns to the first server if it is available. The health check fails only when both servers are unavailable. This avoids a false positive where one remote service endpoint is down but the WAN link can still reach the other target.

This is a sequential fallback mechanism, not a promise that both servers are probed simultaneously and averaged. It is also not the same as configuring two independent Performance SLAs. One health check with two servers protects against a single target outage; separate health checks represent different services or independent path measurements. Fortinet also documents that a server can only be used in one Performance SLA at a time.

Configuration and route behavior

In the CLI, the server list is configured under config system sdwan and config health-check. A representative configuration is:

config system sdwan
    config health-check
        edit "internet-path"
            set protocol ping
            set server "198.51.100.10" "203.0.113.20"
            set interval 500
            set failtime 5
            set recoverytime 5
        next
    end
end

Use representative targets and ensure both are reachable through the participants being measured. If one target is reachable only through a different path, the fallback may not prove the health of the intended member. When a member becomes inactive, the Performance SLA can withdraw static routes associated with that interface. Fortinet documents that if multiple static routes use the same interface, they are all withdrawn when the link monitor fails. For SD-WAN load balancing, routes are removed when the member fails all applicable health checks; a single target failure is not enough when the second server remains healthy.

What the GUI does and does not prove

The green server-response arrow indicates that the current probe server responded. It does not prove that latency, jitter or packet-loss targets are satisfied. Inspect the measured quality values and the SLA target separately. A responding server can still be reached over a path that is too slow or lossy for the application. Likewise, a server outage is not necessarily a WAN link outage; it may be a remote endpoint failure, DNS issue, or service maintenance event.

Verification and failure isolation

Use diagnose sys sdwan health-check to inspect the health-check state and current probe behavior. Confirm the two configured server addresses, the active target, participant interfaces, protocol, interval, fail and recovery thresholds. Test the failure cases deliberately: make the first target unavailable while the second remains reachable; then test the reverse; finally make both unavailable. Observe whether the target switches, whether the health check remains up, and when the member or routes are withdrawn.

If a link is marked down while one target responds, check whether the targets belong to the same health-check object or whether the design actually created separate SLAs. If the GUI shows a responding server but the member is excluded, inspect SLA quality thresholds and other health checks. If routes are withdrawn, verify whether all configured health checks on the member have failed and whether static routes are tied to that interface. This separates target availability, path quality, and route installation into distinct diagnostic layers.

Operational design

Choose two independent targets that represent the service and are reachable over each intended participant. Avoid selecting two addresses hosted in the same failure domain; that would defeat the redundancy benefit. Keep thresholds realistic for the application. Tight latency/jitter/loss values can cause flapping, while loose values can leave a poor path in service. The purpose of the second server is to prevent a single target outage from being mistaken for a failed WAN link, not to conceal a genuinely degraded path.
